point_1: Timeboxed Speculate, Collaborate and Learn cycles of typically four to eight weeks, building the system a small piece at a time.
point_2: Each cycle's quality review demonstrates the working software built in it, but releasable software is not mandated at the end of every cycle. Final Q/A and release is the last stage.
sources: Highsmith (2000), Adaptive Software Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: An "iterative and incremental process" with four serial phases.
point_2: At the end of each iteration, a development release that "could potentially be released into production" goes to pre-production staging.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ambler (2006), The Agile Unified Process

point_1: Iterations are usually two weeks to two months long.
point_2: Running, tested code is delivered to real users every few months (required).
sources: Cockburn (2004), Crystal Clear

point_1: The team chooses one of six lifecycles, and Construction runs in iterations or as a continuous flow.
point_2: Construction produces a potentially consumable solution in each iteration, and the Continuous Delivery lifecycles release at the end of each iteration or more often.
sources: Ambler and Lines (2019), Choose Your WoW! | PMI, Disciplined Agile lifecycles

point_1: Developers integrate code into trunk daily, and automated tests keep it "in a deployable state".
point_2: Release and deployment are continuous.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Anastasov and Pavkovic (2025) | Al-Ashmoery et al. (2024) | Kim et al. (2016), The DevOps Handbook

point_1: Project Increments contain Timeboxes of typically two to four weeks.
point_2: Each Timebox ideally delivers a complete, potentially deployable increment, and the Deployment phase brings a baseline into operational use.
sources: Agile Business Consortium (2014), DSDM Agile Project Framework Handbook

point_1: Design by Feature and Build by Feature repeat for small groups of features, each built in two weeks or less.
point_2: Completed features are promoted to the build. Not stated whether they must be releasable.
sources: Palmer and Felsing (2002), A Practical Guide to Feature-Driven Development

point_1: No iterations or timeboxes, and work flows on a board from ideation to deployment.
point_2: The team produces constantly, "developing only the items which are requested by the customer".
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ladas (2009), Scrumban | Anderson (2010), Kanban

point_1: Scrum sprints of 1 to 4 weeks, with DevOps adding automation and continuous delivery.
point_2: Following Scrum, each sprint is expected to produce an increment, which the Architecture Owner evaluates at the sprint review, and the operations cycle covers integration testing, release and deployment.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2026), Information and Software Technology 190

point_1: One product-level Sprint for all teams, which start and end it at the same time.
point_2: Each Sprint results in an integrated whole product, a "Potentially Shippable Product Increment".
sources: Larman and Vodde (2016), Large-Scale Scrum | LeSS Rules (2024)

point_1: Phases and milestones are specified in detail, with versioned releases.
point_2: Staged delivery, with the highest-priority features first and others in later releases.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | MSF (2003), Microsoft Solutions Framework 3.0 Overview | Giotis (2007), How to deliver successful IT projects using MSF team model and MSF process model

point_1: Products are delivered in timeboxes within management stages.
point_2: Frequent releases is one of the focus areas, but releasable products are not mandated at the end of every timebox.
sources: Marnada et al. (2022), Procedia Computer Science 197 | AXELOS (2015), PRINCE2 Agile

point_1: Teams work in iterations of typically two weeks, grouped into Program Increments of about 8 to 12 weeks.
point_2: The combined increment of all teams is demonstrated at the end of every iteration, and release is on demand, separate from this cadence.
sources: Leffingwell (2018), SAFe 4.5 Reference Guide | Scaled Agile Framework, Iterations

point_1: Work runs in consecutive Sprints of one month or less (mandatory).
point_2: Each Sprint must produce a usable Increment, and an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends.
sources: Schwaber and Sutherland (2020), The Scrum Guide

point_1: Combines Scrum's sprints, usually two to four weeks, with Kanban's pull system and work-in-progress limits, and not every team keeps fixed sprints.
point_2: Releasable software is not mandated at the end of every iteration or planning cycle, as release dates can be separated from planning.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ladas (2009), Scrumban | Scrum Alliance, What is Scrumban?

point_1: Repeated cycles, each developing and verifying the next-level product, with no cycle length stated.
point_2: Releasable software is not mandated at the end of every cycle. A cycle's next-level product may be requirements or a design, and the spiral ends with the installation of new or modified software.
sources: Boehm (1988), A spiral model of software development and enhancement

point_1: Each development cycle passes four phases, built up in iterations, and ends with a product release to customers.
point_2: Each iteration results in an increment, an internal release.
sources: Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh (1999), The Unified Software Development Process

point_1: A V-shaped variation of the waterfall, where requirements are decomposed down the left leg and components are integrated and verified up the right leg.
point_2: Software is delivered at the end of the deployment, "in the absence of prototypes or other artifacts".
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ruparelia (2010), Software development lifecycle models

point_1: Steps run in sequence from system requirements to operations, with a pilot version built first as an early simulation ("do it twice").
point_2: No intermediate deliveries of working software to users described.
sources: Royce (1970), Managing the development of large software systems

point_1: Development is divided into iterations of 1 to 3 weeks, and the most important features are coded first.
point_2: Iterative versions of the system are released to customers often, as small releases.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Wells (1999), Extreme Programming: A gentle introduction

point_1: Changes are expected and adapted to rather than controlled, and plans are revised between cycles. Not stated whether changes can enter during a running cycle.
point_2: No formal approval process is prescribed. Without explicit trade-off priorities, the executive sponsor is involved in most change decisions.
sources: Highsmith (2000), Adaptive Software Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Change management is "typically part of your requirements management efforts".
point_2: Not stated whether changes need formal approval. Configuration management controls and manages changes to project artifacts.
sources: Ambler (2006), The Agile Unified Process

point_1: Not stated when changed requirements enter. Workshops for product and methodology tuning are held at the start and in the middle of each increment.
point_2: Not stated whether changes need formal approval.
sources: Cockburn (2004), Crystal Clear | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Change is treated as natural, and changing requirements are handled through options the team chooses.
point_2: Formal approval is a team choice. A change control board is one option for stakeholder interaction.
sources: PMI, Address Changing Stakeholder Needs | Ambler and Lines (2019), Choose Your WoW!

point_1: Changes enter at any time through version control and the deployment pipeline, aiming at "continuous business change".
point_2: No external approval is required. Peer review, automated tests and pipeline controls validate each change and can meet segregation of duties.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | DORA, Streamlining change approval

point_1: Change is expected and "actively encouraged" within time and cost, and detail evolves after the high-level baseline set in Foundations.
point_2: The team decides within agreed boundaries, the Business Visionary approves changes to high-level requirements, and changes to overall scope must be formally escalated.
sources: Agile Business Consortium (2014), DSDM Agile Project Framework Handbook

point_1: Requirement changes are handled by updating the features list built at the start of the project.
point_2: Not stated whether changes need formal approval. The project manager has the ultimate say on scope.
sources: Palmer and Felsing (2002), A Practical Guide to Feature-Driven Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: New items are pulled into the system at replenishment, usually weekly, when work-in-progress limits allow.
point_2: No formal change-control approval is prescribed. Items are committed when pulled past the commitment point, after which the team works to deliver them.
sources: Kanban University (2021), Illustrated Essential Kanban Notebook

point_1: Backlog items are prioritized at each sprint planning, so changes enter between sprints of 1 to 4 weeks.
point_2: No formal change-control approval is prescribed for backlog changes. At sprint planning, the Architecture Owner aligns the controls and ALM elements with the next sprint's goals.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2026), Information and Software Technology 190

point_1: Items enter the one Product Backlog and are selected for each Sprint at Sprint Planning.
point_2: No formal change-control approval is prescribed. All prioritization goes through the Product Owner.
sources: LeSS Rules (2024)

point_1: Changes are expected from stakeholders and the team, and milestones give explicit opportunities to adjust the scope.
point_2: Once a baseline is set it is under change control, and features change only with review and approval by both team and customer.
sources: MSF (2003), Microsoft Solutions Framework 3.0 Overview | MSF (2002), MSF Process Model v. 3.1 | Giotis (2007), How to deliver successful IT projects using MSF team model and MSF process model

point_1: Detail is expected to change during delivery, with time and cost fixed and the scope delivered flexed within tolerances.
point_2: Changes within tolerance are handled by the team, and changes beyond tolerance are escalated to the Project Board as exceptions.
sources: Marnada et al. (2022), Procedia Computer Science 197 | AXELOS (2015), PRINCE2 Agile

point_1: Product Management continuously prioritizes features in the Program Kanban and Program Backlog, features are planned at PI Planning, and teams plan each iteration.
point_2: No formal approval is prescribed for each feature change, which is reprioritized at PI and iteration planning. Each epic needs a Lean business case and a go or no-go decision in the Portfolio Kanban.
sources: Leffingwell (2018), SAFe 4.5 Reference Guide

point_1: The Product Backlog is refined continuously, and work for each Sprint is selected at Sprint Planning. During the Sprint, no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal.
point_2: No formal change-control approval is prescribed. The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog through ongoing refinement and collaboration with stakeholders, and Sprint scope may be renegotiated with the Product Owner.
sources: Schwaber and Sutherland (2020), The Scrum Guide

point_1: Planning is triggered on demand, when the queue of ready items falls below an order point. Not stated whether new work can enter during a running iteration.
point_2: No formal change-control approval is prescribed. Explicit team policies set how work is selected and let members decide quickly.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ladas (2009), Scrumban

point_1: Each cycle reassesses objectives, alternatives and risks, so earlier stages can be revisited and functionality deferred to later increments.
point_2: No formal change-control procedure is prescribed for individual changes. Each cycle ends with a review seeking the mutual commitment of all concerned parties to the next cycle.
sources: Boehm (1988), A spiral model of software development and enhancement

point_1: Most requirements are captured in Inception and Elaboration and refined in later iterations.
point_2: Changes are handled in the Configuration and Change Management workflow, and the effect of requirement changes on the software must be traceable.
sources: Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh (1999), The Unified Software Development Process | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Requirements are defined with users at the start, and the model has "poor flexibility to manage ongoing changes in requirements".
point_2: No change approval procedure is prescribed. Anomalies are resolved back at the level of decomposition where they arose.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ruparelia (2010), Software development lifecycle models

point_1: Requirements are expected to be complete at the end of the requirements phase, and revisiting a completed phase is discouraged, though Royce allows iteration with adjacent steps.
point_2: Royce prescribes no approval procedure. Changes raised at the reviews before each next phase may involve a formal change control process.
sources: Royce (1970), Managing the development of large software systems | NASA, SWE-019 Software Life Cycle | IEEE Computer Society (2024), SWEBOK Guide v4.0

point_1: The customer chooses the stories at the planning meeting that starts each iteration, and the release plan is renegotiated every three to five iterations.
point_2: No formal change-control approval is prescribed. Business people decide priorities, and developers estimate the work.
sources: Wells (1999), Extreme Programming: A gentle introduction

point_1: Not stated how often software is released. Final quality assurance and release close the project.
point_2: Timeboxed cycles of about four to eight weeks.
sources: Highsmith (2000), Adaptive Software Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Development releases go to pre-production staging at the end of each iteration, and production releases follow, for example every six months.
point_2: Iterations of two weeks.
sources: Ambler (2006), The Agile Unified Process | Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3)

point_1: Running, tested code is delivered to real users every few months, and increments last at most four months.
point_2: Iterations are usually two weeks to two months long.
sources: Cockburn (2004), Crystal Clear | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: The Continuous Delivery lifecycles release at the end of each iteration or more often, and the Agile and Lean lifecycles release in a Transition phase.
point_2: Iteration length is chosen by the team, and the Lean lifecycles work without iterations.
sources: Ambler and Lines (2019), Choose Your WoW! | PMI, Disciplined Agile lifecycles

point_1: Continuous release and deployment, with the ability to release "with high velocity".
point_2: No iterations stated.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3)

point_1: Deployment at the end of a Project Increment, of the final solution or a subset of it.
point_2: Timeboxes of typically two to four weeks.
sources: Agile Business Consortium (2014), DSDM Agile Project Framework Handbook

point_1: Not stated how often software is released. Completed features are promoted to the main build.
point_2: Each iteration takes from a few days to a maximum of two weeks.
sources: Palmer and Felsing (2002), A Practical Guide to Feature-Driven Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Not stated as a fixed interval. Deliveries are planned in delivery planning meetings.
point_2: No iterations or timeboxes.
sources: Kanban University (2021), Illustrated Essential Kanban Notebook | Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3)

point_1: Not stated how often software is released. Release and deployment follow integration testing in the operations cycle, with continuous delivery.
point_2: Sprints of 1 to 4 weeks.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2026), Information and Software Technology 190

point_1: Not stated how often software is released. The perfection goal is a shippable product each Sprint, "or even more frequently".
point_2: One product-level Sprint, which all teams start and end at the same time.
sources: LeSS Rules (2024)

point_1: Versioned releases, with the time between versions set by the size and type of project and by customer needs.
point_2: Not stated how long iterations last.
sources: MSF (2002), MSF Process Model v. 3.1 | Giotis (2007), How to deliver successful IT projects using MSF team model and MSF process model

point_1: Frequent releases is one of the focus areas. Not stated how often.
point_2: Work is done in timeboxes within management stages. Not stated how long a timebox lasts.
sources: Marnada et al. (2022), Procedia Computer Science 197 | AXELOS (2015), PRINCE2 Agile

point_1: Release on demand, decoupled from the development cadence, with timing as a business decision.
point_2: Iterations of typically two weeks, within Program Increments of about 8 to 12 weeks.
sources: Scaled Agile Framework, Release on Demand | Scaled Agile Framework, Iterations | Leffingwell (2018), SAFe 4.5 Reference Guide

point_1: Not stated how often software is released. Increments may be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends.
point_2: Sprints of fixed length, one month or less (mandatory).
sources: Schwaber and Sutherland (2020), The Scrum Guide

point_1: Release dates can be separated from planning, with a feature freeze and triage before a release date.
point_2: Sprints are usually two to four weeks, but not every team keeps fixed sprints.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ladas (2009), Scrumban | Scrum Alliance, What is Scrumban?

point_1: Not stated how often software is released. The spiral ends with the installation of new or modified software.
point_2: Not stated how long a cycle lasts.
sources: Boehm (1988), A spiral model of software development and enhancement

point_1: A product release ends each development cycle, with a beta release in Transition.
point_2: Iterations vary from two weeks or less up to six months.
sources: Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh (1999), The Unified Software Development Process | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Software is delivered at the end of the deployment.
point_2: No iterations stated.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3)

point_1: One delivery at the end, with operations as the last step of the sequence.
point_2: No delivery cycles. A pilot version is built first, and the version delivered to the customer is the second.
sources: Royce (1970), Managing the development of large software systems

point_1: Iterative versions of the system are released to customers often, as small releases.
point_2: Iterations of 1 to 3 weeks.
sources: Wells (1999), Extreme Programming: A gentle introduction

point_1: Mission artifacts, the project vision, project data sheet and product specification outline, with the data sheet as the minimum deliverable.
point_2: ASD gives "a framework of concepts, practices, and guidelines" rather than prescriptive rules, and work is done through team collaboration.
sources: Highsmith (2000), Adaptive Software Development

point_1: Models and documents "just barely good enough", with the process described in "a handful of pages".
point_2: The AUP assumes "Your staff knows what they're doing", and the process can be tailored.
sources: Ambler (2006), The Agile Unified Process

point_1: About twenty work products are listed, with tolerance on their form.
point_2: The team adjusts its own way of working in reflection workshops (required).
sources: Cockburn (2004), Crystal Clear | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: No fixed document set. Teams choose artifacts from the options in each process goal.
point_2: The team chooses its own way of working, guided by the process goals.
sources: Ambler and Lines (2019), Choose Your WoW!

point_1: No mandatory documents stated.
point_2: Not stated who decides how to work. Development and operations share responsibility for the service.
sources: Kim et al. (2016), The DevOps Handbook

point_1: Products such as the Business Case and Prioritised Requirements List, with their formality decided per project.
point_2: The team is empowered to decide within the boundaries agreed in Foundations.
sources: Agile Business Consortium (2014), DSDM Agile Project Framework Handbook

point_1: Five processes produce an overall object model, a features list and a plan by feature, then design and build per feature.
point_2: The project manager has the ultimate say on scope, schedule and staffing, and chief programmers lead feature teams of class owners.
sources: Palmer and Felsing (2002), A Practical Guide to Feature-Driven Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: No mandatory documents. A board, work-in-progress limits and explicit policies.
point_2: Start with what you do now and respect existing roles, and "Manage the work, let people self-organize around it".
sources: Kanban University (2021), Illustrated Essential Kanban Notebook

point_1: IT controls and ALM elements, from the business case and specifications to the test book, kept in the IS audit hub throughout the project.
point_2: Scrum teams with a Product Owner and Scrum Master, and an Architecture Owner who keeps the controls and ALM elements aligned with IT governance.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2026), Information and Software Technology 190

point_1: No documents beyond one Product Backlog, one Definition of Done and the teams' Sprint Backlogs.
point_2: Self-managing teams decide how to do their items and decide cross-team coordination, and managers are optional.
sources: LeSS Rules (2024) | Larman and Vodde (2016), Large-Scale Scrum

point_1: Each phase produces documents, such as a vision/scope document, functional specification and master project plan and schedule.
point_2: A team of peers makes major decisions jointly, and program management orchestrates the process in each phase.
sources: MSF (2003), Microsoft Solutions Framework 3.0 Overview | MSF (2002), MSF Process Model v. 3.1 | Giotis (2007), How to deliver successful IT projects using MSF team model and MSF process model

point_1: Management products such as the business case, plans and registers, tailored in form, with all seven principles kept.
point_2: Delivery teams self-organize within work packages and tolerances agreed with the project manager.
sources: Marnada et al. (2022), Procedia Computer Science 197 | AXELOS (2015), PRINCE2 Agile

point_1: Artifacts at each level, such as backlogs, PI objectives, Vision, Roadmap and Solution Intent.
point_2: Teams plan their own iterations within PI objectives, and Product Management prioritizes the features.
sources: Leffingwell (2018), SAFe 4.5 Reference Guide

point_1: Three artifacts, the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment, each with a commitment.
point_2: The Scrum Team is self-managing and decides internally who does what, when and how.
sources: Schwaber and Sutherland (2020), The Scrum Guide

point_1: No mandatory documents stated.
point_2: The team controls its own workload through explicit team policies.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3)

point_1: No fixed document set. Detail is added only where its absence would jeopardize the project.
point_2: Not stated who decides how to work. Each cycle plans the next phases according to risk.
sources: Boehm (1988), A spiral model of software development and enhancement

point_1: Thirty roles, called workers, with artifacts and models for each of nine workflows.
point_2: The project manager plans each iteration within the phase plan.
sources: Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh (1999), The Unified Software Development Process | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: Specific deliverables are "expected in each phase".
point_2: Not stated who decides how to work. The model is used in "tightly controlled development processes".
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Sommerville (2008), The V-model of software development

point_1: Six documents, under "ruthless enforcement of documentation requirements".
point_2: Management decides, for example when final checkout is done and by whom. No team decision rights stated.
sources: Royce (1970), Managing the development of large software systems

point_1: Only the code and the tests are kept as permanent artifacts, and other documents are generated from them.
point_2: Business people make business decisions and technical people technical ones, and developers sign up for and estimate their own tasks.
sources: Beck and Andres (2004), Extreme Programming Explained, 2nd ed. | Wells (1999), Extreme Programming: A gentle introduction

point_1: At the end of each cycle, in quality reviews with customer focus groups, technical reviews and project postmortems.
point_2: From customers and the team, and the plan is revised for the next cycle.
sources: Highsmith (2000), Adaptive Software Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: At the end of each iteration, when a development release goes to pre-production staging and notes are taken on what works.
point_2: Customers are involved in development. Not stated how feedback feeds the plan.
sources: Ambler (2006), The Agile Unified Process | Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3)

point_1: Reflection workshops in each increment and two user viewings per release, as mandatory policy standards.
point_2: From users and the team, and the workshops tune both the product and the methodology.
sources: Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis | Cockburn (2004), Crystal Clear

point_1: Demos, from scheduled iteration demos to on-demand or all-hands demos, are options the team chooses.
point_2: From stakeholders, and demos are listed as ways to elicit requirements, so they feed the work.
sources: PMI, Address Changing Stakeholder Needs | PMI, Govern Delivery Team

point_1: Continuously, through monitoring in production, automated tests in the pipeline and post-incident reviews.
point_2: From operations, tests and users, and production telemetry feeds development work.
sources: Kim et al. (2016), The DevOps Handbook

point_1: At the end of each Timebox, through demonstrations and acceptance by the Business Ambassador, and in a retrospective for each Project Increment.
point_2: From business roles and the team, and the Business Case is formally reviewed at the end of each Project Increment.
sources: Agile Business Consortium (2014), DSDM Agile Project Framework Handbook

point_1: Domain walkthroughs before design, and design and code inspections in every feature iteration.
point_2: From domain experts and inspectors. Not stated how feedback changes the plan.
sources: Palmer and Felsing (2002), A Practical Guide to Feature-Driven Development | Abrahamsson et al. (2002), Agile software development methods: Review and analysis

point_1: At set cadences, such as a daily Kanban meeting, weekly replenishment, a service delivery review every two weeks and a monthly risk review.
point_2: From the team, customers and managers, and the cadences pass information and change requests to each other, up to strategy.
sources: Kanban University (2021), Illustrated Essential Kanban Notebook | Kanban University, Kanban cadences

point_1: Each sprint has a Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective, and operations add monitoring and feedback.
point_2: The Architecture Owner evaluates the increment at the Sprint Review, and the cycle returns to sprint planning.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2026), Information and Software Technology 190

point_1: Each Sprint has one product Sprint Review for all teams, a retrospective per team and an Overall Retrospective.
point_2: From suitable stakeholders and the teams, for "effective inspection and adaptation".
sources: LeSS Rules (2024)

point_1: At the review of each major milestone, and in a project review and customer satisfaction survey after deployment.
point_2: From the team, customer and stakeholders, and milestone reviews help the team make midcourse corrections.
sources: MSF (2003), Microsoft Solutions Framework 3.0 Overview | MSF (2002), MSF Process Model v. 3.1 | Giotis (2007), How to deliver successful IT projects using MSF team model and MSF process model

point_1: Timebox reviews and retrospectives during delivery, and stage boundaries that review progress and plans.
point_2: From the customer and the team, and the results feed the plans at stage boundaries.
sources: Marnada et al. (2022), Procedia Computer Science 197 | AXELOS (2015), PRINCE2 Agile

point_1: A System Demo in every iteration, and Inspect and Adapt at the end of each Program Increment.
point_2: From ART members and stakeholders, and improvement items go to the ART Backlog for the next PI Planning, while telemetry measures each release.
sources: Leffingwell (2018), SAFe 4.5 Reference Guide | Scaled Agile Framework, Inspect and Adapt | Scaled Agile Framework, Release on Demand

point_1: Each Sprint has a Daily Scrum, a Sprint Review with key stakeholders and a Sprint Retrospective (mandatory).
point_2: From stakeholders and the team, and the Product Backlog may be adjusted at the Sprint Review. No feedback from operations stated.
sources: Schwaber and Sutherland (2020), The Scrum Guide

point_1: Scrum events such as reviews and retrospectives are kept.
point_2: Not stated from whom or how review results feed planning, which is triggered on demand.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Ladas (2009), Scrumban

point_1: At the review that completes each cycle, and through prototyping, simulation, benchmarking and user questionnaires within cycles.
point_2: From the primary people or organizations concerned with the product, and the review covers the plans for the next cycle.
sources: Boehm (1988), A spiral model of software development and enhancement

point_1: At the end of each iteration, in an assessment of its results.
point_2: From the team, and from beta users in Transition, and the assessment feeds the plan for the next iteration.
sources: Jacobson, Booch and Rumbaugh (1999), The Unified Software Development Process

point_1: Each development stage has a related testing stage, whose verification procedures are defined during that development stage.
point_2: Users take part in the initial requirements definition and decide on anomalies found during integration. No feedback from operations stated.
sources: Ruparelia (2010), Software development lifecycle models | Sommerville (2008), The V-model of software development

point_1: At formal customer reviews after preliminary design, after critical design and at final acceptance, and in testing after coding.
point_2: From the customer and test specialists, and test failures can force redesign. No feedback from operations stated.
sources: Royce (1970), Managing the development of large software systems

point_1: Throughout each iteration, with business users and with automated acceptance tests that run often.
point_2: The customer specifies the acceptance tests and sets priorities, and failed tests are scheduled for fixing in each iteration.
sources: Kirpitsas and Pachidis (2022), Software 1(3) | Wells (1999), Extreme Programming: A gentle introduction

point_1: A plan assigns product features to cycles, but links between artefacts are not specified.
point_2: Systematic, bidirectional traceability linking requirements, changes, design, test evidence and releases is not explicitly specified.
sources: Highsmith (2000), Adaptive Software Development

point_1: Configuration management tracks artifact versions over time and controls changes to them.
point_2: Systematic, bidirectional traceability linking requirements, changes, design, test evidence and releases is not explicitly specified.
sources: Ambler (2006), The Agile Unified Process

point_1: Work products include a requirements file, release plan and bug reports, but links between them are not specified.
point_2: Systematic, bidirectional traceability linking requirements, changes, design, test evidence and releases is not explicitly specified.
sources: Cockburn (2004), Crystal Clear

point_1: No links between artefacts are prescribed, and requirements documentation is a team choice, from detailed to high-level.
